pos: n. phrase (civil or political rule, as distinct from the spiritual; and, in controversy, the papal claim to wield both swords)
etymology: Latin temporalis, of time, from tempus, time. Webster already pairs the senses: temporal as opposed to spiritual, and temporal power as secular, civil, or political power. The papal claim is that the church's head holds that sword as well as the spiritual one.
biblical_def: Temporal power is rule in this world: courts, swords, taxes, the things that belong to time. Christ drew the line with a sentence that still judges Rome: “My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight” (John 18:36). He would not be made a king by force: “When Jesus therefore perceived that they would come and take him by force, to make him a king, he departed again into a mountain himself alone” (John 6:15). He refused the divider's bench: “Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?” (Luk 12:14). And He left Caesar his own: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21). The apostle's soldier is not entangled: “No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life” (2Ti 2:4). The civil magistrate is a real ordinance of God. That is not the pope's claim. The pope's claim is that the Vicar of Christ holds both swords, and may depose princes. The New Testament never gives that office to any apostle, still less to a later Roman bishop.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines temporal as pertaining to this life or this world or the body only; secular; opposed to spiritual, and also opposed to ecclesiastical; as temporal power, that is, secular, civil or political power.
webster_full: TEM'PORAL, a. [L. temporalis, from tempus, time.]
1. Pertaining to this life or this world or the body only; secular; as temporal concerns; temporal affairs. In this sense, it is opposed to spiritual.
In this sense also it is opposed to ecclesiastical; as temporal power, that is, secular, civil or political power; temporal courts, those which take cognizance of civil suits.
Temporal jurisdiction is that which regards civil and political affairs.
2. Measured or limited by time, or by this life or this state of things; having limited existence; opposed to eternal.
scriptures: John 18:36
Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
John 6:15
When Jesus therefore perceived that they would come and take him by force, to make him a king, he departed again into a mountain himself alone.
And he said unto him, Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?
No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.
corruption_summary: Rome made the two swords one, and some Protestants then emptied the magistrate of any duty under God at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Unam Sanctam (1302) is the classic papal sentence: two swords, both the pope's, the spiritual to be used by the church and the temporal to be used for the church. John 18:36 will not wear it. If the kingdom were of this world, the servants would fight. They did not. Peter was told to put up the sword. A see that deposes kings and raises armies in Peter's name has already answered Jesus with a no.

The opposite Protestant error is to hear “not of this world” as if Caesar were a neutral zone where God's law has no claim. The dictionary's magistrate is a minister of God, a real ordinance, owed honour in all things lawful. Temporal power belongs to that office, not to the bishop of Rome, and not to a church that has forgotten it. Two kingdoms, properly distinguished, is not Radical Two Kingdoms. The civil sword is God's. It is not the pope's, and it is not nobody's.

John 6:15 is the gospel's own comment on Christian nationalism as a method. They would take Him by force to make Him a king, and He departed. The crown comes at the right hand, not from a crowd with a program. Render to Caesar what is Caesar's. Do not let a pontiff collect it in Christ's name.
roots_summary: Latin temporalis, of time; Greek basileia (G932), kingdom; kosmos (G2889), this world; kōsar, Caesar.
roots_lines: Greek hē basileia hē emē ouk estin ek tou kosmou toutou — My kingdom is not of this world; John 18:36.
Latin potestas temporalis — the civil sword, as distinct from potestas spiritualis.
Greek apodote ta Kaisaros Kaisari (G591) — render the things of Caesar to Caesar; Matthew 22:21.
usage: “My kingdom is not of this world” — if it were, the servants would fight.
“Render therefore unto Caesar” — and unto God the things that are God's, not Peter's successor's.
“Take him by force, to make him a king” — and He departed.

pos: adv. phrase (Latin: outside of us; the location of justifying righteousness, in Christ, not in the believer's infused quality)
etymology: Latin extra, outside, beyond, + nos, us. Reformation shorthand for the alien righteousness: the righteousness by which a sinner is justified is Christ's, counted to him, not a habit poured into him.
biblical_def: Extra nos names where the righteousness that justifies is found: outside the sinner, in Christ. Paul will not be found in his own: “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith” (Php 3:9). David had already sung the same location: “the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works” (Rom 4:6). The exchange is in another: “he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2Co 5:21). Isaiah's picture is clothing, not infusion: “he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness” (Isa 61:10). And the verdict is free: “Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom 3:24). In Him. Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Not in a quality the sinner has begun to possess. That is the whole Reformation in two Latin words.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for the Latin phrase. Extra nos is Reformation shorthand: the righteousness that justifies is Christ's, outside the sinner, imputed, not a habit infused within.
webster_full: EXTRA NOS, Latin, outside of us. Reformation theological phrase, not an 1828 English headword.
The righteousness by which a man is justified is not in him as a poured quality. It is Christ's, counted to him.
Opposite of infused righteousness as the ground of the verdict.
Luther, Melanchthon, and the Protestant scholastics used the phrase to keep justification from sliding back into a change of the sinner's interior as its ground.
scriptures: Php 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
Rom 4:6
Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works,
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.

I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.
Rom 3:24
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:
corruption_summary: Rome puts the righteousness inside the man as a habit, and then the verdict waits on the habit. The gospel puts it in Christ, and the verdict is already spoken.
corruption_paragraphs: Tridentine justification is not extra nos. It is a process in which grace is infused, cooperation begins, and the man becomes formally righteous by an interior gift. Philippians 3:9 will not have two righteousnesses mixed into one ground. Paul will be found in Him, not having his own. A righteousness that is of the law, even a Spirit-assisted law-keeping, is still his own. Extra nos is the refusal of that mixture.

The evangelical corruption is quieter. Justification is still preached as a verdict, and then assurance is quietly relocated to the quality of the inner life. When a man looks at his sanctification to find out whether he is justified, he has crawled back inside himself. Romans 4:6 is blessedness without works. The robe in Isaiah 61:10 is put on him. He did not grow it.

Sanctification is real, and it is inside us. That is why the phrase has to be kept for justification. Confusing the two is how Rome and how a nervous Protestant end up in the same place: looking in the mirror for a righteousness God located in His Son.
roots_summary: Latin extra nos, outside us; Greek logizomai (G3049), to impute; dikaiosynē (G1343), righteousness; en autō, in him.
roots_lines: Latin extra nos — outside us; the Protestant scholastic location of justifying righteousness.
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to impute, count; Romans 4:6, 4:5, 4:24.
Greek en autō (G1722) — in him; 2 Corinthians 5:21, the righteousness of God in Christ, not in the sinner.
usage: “Not having mine own righteousness” — the man will be found in Him.
“Imputeth righteousness without works” — outside, counted, not grown.
“Covered me with the robe of righteousness” — put on, not infused as the verdict's ground.

pos: n. (a man who turns Christian liberty into license; historically also a Roman freedman, then a name for the dissolute)
etymology: Latin libertinus, a freedman, from liber, free. Webster still records the Roman sense, then the moral one: one who lives without restraint of the animal passion. In church controversy the word names the man who treats grace as a permit.
biblical_def: A libertine, in the church's use, is not merely a rake. He is a man who has a doctrine of liberty and uses it as a cloak. Jude saw him come in by the side door: “ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ” (Jude 4). Paul had already drawn the rail: “ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another” (Gal 5:13). Peter says the same with the servant's name still on: “As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God” (1Pe 2:16). The rhetorical question is the test: “Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?” (Rom 6:1). And the false teachers' advertisement is still running: “While they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption” (2Pe 2:19). Christian liberty is real. The libertine is the man who cashes it at the flesh's window.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines libertine as, among the Romans, a freedman; then as one who lives without restraint of the animal passion; a rake; and, as an adjective, licentious, dissolute, not under the restraint of law or religion.
webster_full: LIB'ERTINE, n. [L. libertinus, from liber, free.]
1. Among the Romans, a freedman; a person manumitted or set free from legal servitude.
2. One unconfined; one free from restraint.
3. A man who lives without restraint of the animal passion; one who indulges his lust without restraint; one who leads a dissolute, licentious life; a rake; a debauchee.
LIB'ERTINE, a. Licentious; dissolute; not under the restraint of law or religion; as libertine principles; a libertine life.
scriptures: Jude 4

For there are certain men crept in unawares, who were before of old ordained to this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ.
Gal 5:13
For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.
As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God.
Rom 6:1
What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
While they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption: for of whom a man is overcome, of the same is he brought in bondage.
corruption_summary: Grace is preached as if Romans 6:1 were a lifestyle recommendation, and the old word libertine is retired so the thing can be called authenticity.
corruption_paragraphs: Jude 4 is not about pagans who never heard of grace. It is men crept in, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness. The raw material is the gospel. The product is license. A pulpit that will not say no to that trade is already in the traffic. Galatians 5:13 was written to people who had the Spirit. Liberty is not the dispute. The use of it is.

The modern rename is authenticity, or being true to desire, or refusing legalism. 1 Peter 2:16 had the rename already: a cloke of maliciousness. The cloak is the point. The man still wants to be called a servant of God while he uses freedom as cover. Peter will not let him keep both.

The other error is to hear the warning and then cage the church in new laws Christ did not give. The cure for the libertine is not a second Sinai of house rules. It is Romans 6: the man who died with Christ does not continue in sin that grace may abound. Servants of God, not servants of corruption. 2 Peter 2:19 says the advertisers of liberty are themselves slaves. Believe the fruit, not the brochure.
roots_summary: Latin libertinus, freedman; Greek eleutheria (G1657), liberty; aselgeia (G766), lasciviousness; epikalumma (G1942), a cloak.
roots_lines: Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty; Galatians 5:13, 1 Peter 2:16, 2 Peter 2:19.
Greek aselgeia (G766) — lasciviousness; Jude 4, the thing grace is turned into.
Greek epikalumma (G1942) — a cloak; 1 Peter 2:16, liberty used as cover.
usage: “Turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness” — crept in, not standing outside.
“Use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh” — the rail, not the repeal of liberty.
“They promise them liberty” — and are themselves servants of corruption.

pos: n. pl. (the Family of Love: a sixteenth-century sect of inner-light religion, condemned by the Reformed as dissolving law, church, and the letter of Scripture)
etymology: From the Familia Caritatis, the Family of Love, gathered around Hendrik Niclaes in the sixteenth century. English controversy shortened the members to Familists. The name is not in the Authorized Version. The shape of the error is: a form of godliness, an inner word set over the written one.
biblical_def: Familists names a historical people, the Family of Love, and a recurring pattern: an inner revelation that quietly retires the written Word, the moral law, and the visible church. Scripture had the pattern before Niclaes. “Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away” (2Ti 3:5). Peter said false teachers would come, “who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them” (2Pe 2:1). John required a test, not a feeling: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jn 4:1). Paul warned against a religion of unseen things and voluntary humility: “worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind” (Col 2:18). And the Spirit had already said that some would “depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils” (1Ti 4:1). The Family of Love is one historical dress of that departure. The letter of Scripture is not a husk the spiritual man outgrows.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for Familists. The Family of Love was a sixteenth-century sect; English Protestants used the name for those who set an inner word above the written Word and treated the moral law as a lower stage.
webster_full: FAMILISTS, n. Members of the Family of Love (Familia Caritatis), a sixteenth-century sect associated with Hendrik Niclaes.
Not an 1828 English headword. English Reformed and Puritan controversy used the name for inner-light religion that dissolved the authority of the written Word.
The charge, whether in every particular just of every adherent, was antinomian: the spiritual man above the law, the church, and the letter.
The biblical pattern is older than the sect: a form of godliness, seducing spirits, and a beguiling of the reward by things unseen.
scriptures: Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.

But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Col 2:18
Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,
Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils;
corruption_summary: The Family of Love is mostly forgotten; the method is not. An inner word that cannot be tried by the written one is still the same sect without the name.
corruption_paragraphs: Niclaes taught a family of the elect who had come into a stage beyond ordinary Christian profession. The written Word, the sacraments, and the magistrate's religion were treated as shadows for the simple. Colossians 2:18 already named the puffing up: a man intruding into what he hath not seen. 1 John 4:1 forbids the shortcut. Spirits are to be tried. A revelation that will not sit for that exam is not from God, whatever love it puts in the title.

The Reformed polemic against Familists was not a dislike of affection. It was the defence of the moral law and of the ordinary means. 2 Timothy 3:5 is the diagnostic: form of godliness, power denied. A group can speak constantly of love and still deny the Lord that bought them, which is Peter's charge in 2 Peter 2:1. The dictionary will not baptize a historical sect, and it will not pretend the pattern died with Elizabeth's proclamations against them.

Today the same grain appears wherever “what the Spirit is saying to me” is not allowed to be corrected by what the Spirit already said in Scripture. The Family of Love was one name. The command is the same: from such turn away. Try the spirits. Do not be beguiled of your reward by a humility that will not be taught.
roots_summary: Latin Familia Caritatis; Greek morphōsis eusebeias (G3446, G2150), form of godliness; dokimazō (G1381), to try; planaō related seduction.
roots_lines: Greek morphōsis eusebeias (G3446, G2150) — a form of godliness; 2 Timothy 3:5.
Greek dokimazete ta pneumata (G1381) — try the spirits; 1 John 4:1.
Latin Familia Caritatis — Family of Love; the historical name behind English Familists.
usage: “A form of godliness, but denying the power thereof” — from such turn away.
“Try the spirits whether they are of God” — an inner word that will not sit for the exam is not from Him.
“Intruding into those things which he hath not seen” — the puffing up Colossians already named.

pos: n. phrase (Rome's interior gift of justice, treated as the formal cause of justification; not the imputed righteousness of Christ)
etymology: Latin infundere, to pour in. Infused righteousness is justice poured into the soul as a habit. The Reformation's counter-word is imputed: counted, not poured, as the ground of the verdict.
biblical_def: Infused righteousness is the Roman account of how a man is made just: grace is poured into him, a habit of justice is created, and on that interior gift — with his cooperation — he is counted righteous. The Authorized Version locates the verdict elsewhere. “But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness” (Rom 4:5). The man in view is ungodly when he is justified. A habit of justice cannot be the formal cause of that sentence. “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28). Paul will not even let a Christian's own Spirit-wrought deeds into the ground: “a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16). He will be found “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ” (Php 3:9). And David describes “the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works” (Rom 4:6). Infusion as sanctification is not in dispute. Infusion as the thing that justifies is another gospel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines infuse as to pour in, as a liquid, and to instill, as principles or qualities. Infused righteousness takes that pouring as the ground of God's verdict. The Scriptures use counting, not pouring, for that verdict.
webster_full: INFU'SE, v.t. [L. infusus, infundo, to pour in; in and fundo, to pour.]
1. To pour in, as a liquid.
2. To instill, as principles or qualities.
4. To introduce; as, to infuse Gallicisms into a composition.
The theological phrase infused righteousness is not Webster's headword. It names Rome's poured interior justice as the formal cause of justification.
scriptures: Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
Php 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
Rom 4:6
Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works,
corruption_summary: If the verdict waits on a poured quality, the ungodly cannot be justified, and Romans 4:5 has to be rewritten as a man already being made godly.
corruption_paragraphs: Trent made infused righteousness the formal cause of justification. The man is not counted just by Christ's righteousness extra nos. He is made just by a grace in him, and he must cooperate. Romans 4:5 will not survive that. God justifieth the ungodly. Faith is counted for righteousness to the man who worketh not. If a habit of justice were the cause, the man would not be ungodly at the moment of the verdict, and Paul would have said so.

Protestant slides toward the same place by making justification a process of becoming. Galatians 2:16 was written to people who already believed, to stop them adding the law back into the ground. Infused righteousness as sanctification is what the Spirit actually does. The corruption is using that real work as the title to the court. Philippians 3:9 keeps two righteousnesses distinct: mine own, of the law; and God's, through the faith of Christ. Mixing them is how you lose both the verdict and the holiness.

The pastoral fruit of the Roman construction is never-finished assurance. If the habit can be lost, the verdict can be lost. Romans 4:6's blessedness is without works. That is not a permission to be lawless. It is the only ground on which a man can then obey without using his obedience as currency.
roots_summary: Latin iustitia infusa; Greek logizomai (G3049), to count; dikaioō (G1344), to justify; asebēs (G765), ungodly.
roots_lines: Greek logizomai (G3049) — counted, imputed; Romans 4:5, 4:6 — the verb infusion cannot replace.
Greek asebē (G765) — the ungodly; Romans 4:5, the one God justifies.
Latin iustitia infusa — infused justice; Trent's formal cause, against the Protestant iustitia imputata.
usage: “Him that justifieth the ungodly” — not the man already made just inside.
“Justified by faith without the deeds of the law” — including Spirit-assisted deeds as ground.
“Imputeth righteousness without works” — counted, not poured, as the verdict.

pos: n. (in divinity, grief for sin from fear of punishment, as distinct from contrition; the sorrow of the world that worketh death)
etymology: Latin attritio, a rubbing, from atterere, to rub against. Webster's third sense is the theological one: grief for sin arising from fear of punishment; the lowest degree of repentance. The word is the church's name for Judas's tears as against David's.
biblical_def: Attrition is grief for sin that has not yet reached God. Webster recorded the divine's use: grief arising from fear of punishment, the lowest degree of repentance. Scripture had already split the thing in two. “For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death” (2Co 7:10). Judas is the exhibit: “when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver” (Mat 27:3). He repented himself. He did not repent unto God. Esau sought the blessing with tears and “found no place of repentance” (Heb 12:17). Contrast David, who will not stop at consequences: “Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight” (Psa 51:4). And the sacrifice God will not despise is “a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart” (Psa 51:17). Attrition may be the first rubbing. It is not yet the broken heart. Rome sometimes treated attrition plus the sacrament as enough. Paul called the sorrow of the world death.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines attrition as abrasion, the act of wearing by friction; and, with divines, grief for sin arising from fear of punishment; the lowest degree of repentance.
webster_full: ATTRI'TION, n.
1. Abrasion; the act of wearing by friction, or rubbing substances together.
2. The state of being worn.
3. With divines, grief for sin arising from fear of punishment; the lowest degree of repentance.
scriptures: For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
Mat 27:3
Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders,
For ye know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected: for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.
Psa 51:4
Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
corruption_summary: Fear of hell is treated either as sufficient repentance, or as an illegitimate motive, and both miss 2 Corinthians 7:10's split.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome's pastoral machinery could treat attrition — fear of punishment, without the love of God yet — as adequate matter for the sacrament, the sacrament then supplying what the heart lacked. 2 Corinthians 7:10 will not have a sorrow that worketh death baptized into a sorrow that worketh salvation. Judas repented himself. The verb is in Matthew. The fruit was a hanging, not a restoration. Tears are not the test. The object of the sorrow is.

The evangelical reverse is to scold any mention of fear as an unworthy motive, as if the beginning of wisdom were a problem to be grown out of. Proverbs is not ashamed of fear. Attrition is not illegitimate as a first blow. It is insufficient as a finished repentance. David starts with the wound toward God: against thee, thee only. A ministry that cannot say “flee from the wrath to come” has already decided that the sorrow of the world is the only kind it respects, just with better lighting.

Hebrews 12:17 is the warning against waiting. Esau sought carefully with tears and found no place of repentance. Attrition can be loud and late. Contrition is a broken heart while it is still called today. Do not baptize fear as the whole of repentance. Do not despise it as if it were not even a beginning.
roots_summary: Latin attritio, a rubbing; Greek lypē (G3077), sorrow; metanoia (G3341), repentance; metamelomai (G3338), to regret; Hebrew nakeh / dakah, broken, contrite.
roots_lines: Greek kata theon lypē vs tou kosmou lypē (G3077) — godly sorrow vs the sorrow of the world; 2 Corinthians 7:10.
Greek metamelomai (G3338) — to regret, repent oneself; Matthew 27:3, Judas.
Hebrew lev nishbar venidkeh — a broken and a contrite heart; Psalm 51:17, the thing attrition has not yet become.
usage: “The sorrow of the world worketh death” — Judas's verb, not David's.
“Repented himself” — himself, not unto God.
“Against thee, thee only, have I sinned” — the object that makes sorrow godly.

pos: n. phrase (Molina's scientia media: a supposed divine knowledge of what free creatures would do in any circumstance, used to keep sovereignty and libertarian freedom both intact)
etymology: English for Latin scientia media, middle knowledge, so called because it was placed between God's knowledge of mere possibles and His knowledge of what He has decreed. Luis de Molina (16th c.) framed it so that God's decree could wait on what the creature would freely do.
biblical_def: Middle knowledge is the Jesuit device by which God is said to know, before He decrees, what every free creature would do in any given world, so that He can pick a world in which they freely do what He wants. Scripture never gives Him that waiting-room. “Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure” (Isa 46:10). The cross itself is not a fortunate outcome God foresaw in a creature's hypothetical: “Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain” (Act 2:23). Determinate counsel and wicked hands in one sentence, without a middle science to keep the hands undetermined. “Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world” (Act 15:18). And the unformed substance is already written: “in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them” (Psa 139:16). Even election is “not of works, but of him that calleth” (Rom 9:11). A God whose decree is built on creaturely woulds is not the I AM who does all His pleasure.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines knowledge as a clear and certain perception of that which exists, or of truth and fact, and says God has a perfect knowledge of all his works. He does not grant a third chamber of would-counterfactuals between possibility and decree. That chamber is Molina's.
webster_full: KNOWL'EDGE, n. A clear and certain perception of that which exists, or of truth and fact.
We can have no knowledge of that which does not exist. God has a perfect knowledge of all his works. Human knowledge is very limited, and is mostly gained by observation and experience.
2. Learning; illumination of mind.
Middle knowledge is not Webster's headword. It is the English for Molina's scientia media: God's supposed knowledge of counterfactuals of creaturely freedom, prior to the decree.
scriptures: Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
Act 2:23
Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain:
Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world.
Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them.
Rom 9:11
(For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth;)
corruption_summary: Middle knowledge keeps a libertarian creature by making God's decree a selection among woulds, which is to put the creature's hypothetical will under the counsel that Isaiah says shall stand.
corruption_paragraphs: Give Molina his problem. If God determines what the creature will do, how is the creature free in the Jesuit sense? If God only foresees, how does He govern? Scientia media offers a third: God knows what they would do, and chooses the circumstances. Isaiah 46:10 does not describe a God selecting among creaturely scripts. My counsel shall stand. I will do all my pleasure. The woulds are not the floor. The pleasure is.

Acts 2:23 is the text that should have killed the system. Determinate counsel and wicked hands. The freedom of the crucifiers is not a libertarian exemption God had to work around by middle knowledge. It is compatible with the counsel that delivered Him. The dictionary's standard is the decree, not a warehouse of counterfactuals. Molinism is named in order to be refused, not to be baptised as a Reformed option.

Pastoral Molinism shows up as “God looked down the corridor of time.” That is ordinary foreknowledge talk, and it is already too small. Acts 15:18 is all His works known from the beginning. Psalm 139:16 has the days written when there was none of them. The ungodly are justified by a God who calls, not by a God who found a world in which they would cooperate. Romans 9:11 shut that door before Molina opened a window.
roots_summary: Latin scientia media; Greek hōrismenē boulē (G3724, G1012), determinate counsel; prognōsis (G4268), foreknowledge; Hebrew etsah (H6098), counsel.
roots_lines: Latin scientia media — middle knowledge; Molina, between knowledge of possibles and knowledge of the decreed.
Greek hōrismenē boulē kai prognōsei tou theou — determinate counsel and foreknowledge; Acts 2:23.
Hebrew etsati taqum (H6098) — my counsel shall stand; Isaiah 46:10.
usage: “My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure” — not all my selections among woulds.
“Determinate counsel and foreknowledge” — and wicked hands, in one sentence.
“Not of works, but of him that calleth” — the children not yet born, before any would.

pos: n. (the doctrine that created things never truly cause; God alone acts, and creatures are only the occasions of His acting)
etymology: From occasion: the creature is said to be the occasion, not the cause. The classic modern statement is Malebranche's. The motive is to protect God's immediacy. The cost is to make second causes theatre.
biblical_def: Occasionalism says that fire does not burn, and the will does not choose: God alone causes, and the creature is a cue. Scripture will not empty the creature that way, and it will not make the creature independent either. The Son is “upholding all things by the word of his power” (Heb 1:3). “He is before all things, and by him all things consist” (Col 1:17). “For in him we live, and move, and have our being” (Act 17:28). The Spirit is sent, and things are created: “Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created: and thou renewest the face of the earth” (Psa 104:30). And yet a sparrow falls, and it is still a sparrow falling: “Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father” (Mat 10:29). The fall is real. The without-your-Father is also real. Reformed orthodoxy holds concurrence: God as first cause, creatures as real second causes, neither cancelled. Occasionalism keeps the first and discards the second. Deism keeps a world that runs and forgets the upholding. Both miss the verse that has both.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no headword for occasionalism. The doctrine is modern-philosophical: created agents are occasions of divine action, not true causes. The Scriptures uphold all things by His power without turning the sparrow's fall into a puppet-show.
webster_full: OCCASIONALISM, n. A philosophical doctrine, not an 1828 English headword.
The teaching that finite things do not truly cause effects; God is the sole cause, and creatures supply only the occasion of His acting.
Associated especially with Malebranche. A motive to honour God's immediacy that pays by denying real second causes.
The Reformed alternative is concurrence or concursus: God upholds and concurs with real creaturely causation.
scriptures: Heb 1:3

Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;
Col 1:17
And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.
For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.
Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created: and thou renewest the face of the earth.
Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father.
corruption_summary: Either God does everything so that we do nothing, or we do everything so that God is a spectator. Hebrews 1:3 and Matthew 10:29 refuse both.
corruption_paragraphs: Occasionalism can sound pious. If God is all in all, then let no creature steal the credit. But then Joseph's brothers did not sell him; God merely acted when they seemed to. The Bible is not embarrassed to say both. You meant it for evil; God meant it for good. Second causes are not a threat to the first. They are His ordinary way. A metaphysics that cannot say “the brothers sold him” has stopped reading Genesis.

The pastoral form is fatalism with a holy name. Prayer becomes theatre, because the occasion was going to be used anyway. Means become theatre. Hebrews 1:3 is not theatre. He upholds all things by the word of His power, and the same verse has Him purging our sins. The world is not a screen. It is a creation that consists by Him (Col 1:17) while remaining a world in which sparrows fall and fathers are not absent.

Deism is the other ditch, and it is more popular: a God who wound the clock. Acts 17:28 will not have it. In Him we live and move and have our being, present tense. The dictionary's word is providence, and concurrence under it. Occasionalism is named so it can be refused without sliding into a clockwork heaven.
roots_summary: Latin occasio, occasion; Greek pherō (G5342), to uphold; synistēmi (G4921), to consist; Hebrew barah / chadash in Psalm 104.
roots_lines: Greek pherōn ta panta (G5342) — upholding all things; Hebrews 1:3.
Greek synestēken (G4921) — consist, hold together; Colossians 1:17.
Greek aneu tou patros hymōn — without your Father; Matthew 10:29, the sparrow's real fall, not without Him.
usage: “Upholding all things by the word of his power” — not replacing them with a puppet-show.
“By him all things consist” — they are things, and they consist.
“Shall not fall on the ground without your Father” — a real fall, and not without Him.

pos: n. (a stable disposition of soul; in scholastic use, the infused habits of grace; in Reformed use, real sanctification as fruit, not the ground of justification)
etymology: Latin habitus, a having, a condition, from habere, to have. Webster's habit is the English: a disposition acquired by custom, or a particular state of body or mind. The schoolmen used habitus for a quality that disposes the soul to act. Rome made an infused habitus of justice the formal cause of justification. The Reformed kept the word for sanctification and refused it as the verdict's ground.
biblical_def: Habitus, in the schools, is a stable bent of the soul, a having that disposes a man to act. Scripture is not allergic to real change inside the man. “That by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust” (2Pe 1:4). The Spirit bears fruit, not a theatre of occasions: “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith” (Gal 5:22). Freedom from sin has fruit: “ye have your fruit unto holiness, and the end everlasting life” (Rom 6:22). There is a new man to put on: “the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness” (Eph 4:24). And in Christ, “he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new” (2Co 5:17). The Reformed do not deny the habitus of grace as sanctification. They refuse to make that interior having the righteousness by which a man is justified. Fruit is real. Fruit is not the title.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines habit as garb; as a particular state of body; and as a disposition of mind or body acquired by custom or frequent repetition. The scholastic habitus is that having as a quality of soul. Rome infused it as justifying justice. The Reformed locate it in sanctification.
webster_full: HAB'IT, n. [L. habitus, from habeo, to have to hold.]
3. State of any thing; implying some continuance or permanence; temperament or particular state of a body.
4. A disposition or condition of the mind or body acquired by custom or a frequent repetition of the same act. Habit is that which is held or retained, the effect of custom or frequent repetition.
The Latin habitus in divinity is that stable disposition. Infused habitus as the ground of justification is the Roman construction this dictionary refuses.
scriptures: Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust.
Gal 5:22
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
Rom 6:22
But now being made free from sin, and become servants to God, ye have your fruit unto holiness, and the end everlasting life.
Eph 4:24
And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness.
Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
corruption_summary: Either the interior is made the ground of the verdict, or the interior is treated as optional window-dressing. Peter, Paul, and the fruit of the Spirit will not have either.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome's infused habitus of justice is extra nos refused. If the having in the soul is the formal cause of justification, Romans 4:5's ungodly man disappears. Keep habitus for what 2 Peter 1:4 actually says: partakers of the divine nature, having escaped. That is sanctification, real, inside, by the promises. It is not the robe counted in Romans 4:6.

The cheap-grace reverse treats all talk of a new man as legalism. Ephesians 4:24 says the new man is created after God in righteousness and true holiness, and it is to be put on. Galatians 5:22 is fruit, not a slogan. A gospel that cannot produce a bent of soul toward holiness is not the gospel that frees from sin unto fruit (Rom 6:22). Habitus, in the honest Reformed use, is just that: the Spirit's real work of making a man new, without being asked to justify him.

Do not let the Latin impress you into Rome, and do not let the fear of Rome empty 2 Corinthians 5:17. In Christ he is a new creature. Old things are passed away. That having is not a fiction. It is not the court record either. Keep the offices straight and the word is safe.
roots_summary: Latin habitus, a having; Greek koinōnos physeōs (G2844, G5449), partakers of nature; karpos (G2590), fruit; kainos ktisis (G2537, G2937), new creature.
roots_lines: Latin habitus infusus — infused habit; Rome's interior justice.
Greek theias koinōnoi physeōs (G2304, G2844, G5449) — partakers of the divine nature; 2 Peter 1:4.
Greek karpos tou pneumatos (G2590) — fruit of the Spirit; Galatians 5:22, the visible habitus of grace.
usage: “Partakers of the divine nature” — real inside, not the verdict's ground.
“Fruit unto holiness” — fruit, not the title to the court.
“A new creature” — old things passed away, and still justified extra nos.

pos: n. (Rome's third rank of religious honour: above the dulia of saints, below the latria of God, assigned to Mary; a distinction the second commandment does not know)
etymology: Greek hyper, above, + douleia, service, bondage, religious honour. Medieval Catholic theology ranked latria (God), dulia (saints), and hyperdulia (Mary). The New Testament knows one worship-word for God, and an angel who will not take it.
biblical_def: Hyperdulia is the Roman name for a rank of honour invented to give Mary more than the saints and less than God. The Scriptures do not furnish the rank. “Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve” (Mat 4:10). The first commandment is not a spectrum: “Thou shalt have no other gods before me” (Exo 20:3). The LORD will not share: “my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images” (Isa 42:8). When John fell down before an angel, the angel refused even that: “See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant... worship God” (Rev 19:10). Peter did the same with Cornelius: “Stand up; I myself also am a man” (Act 10:26). If an apostle and an angel will not receive what Rome calls dulia, a third rank called hyperdulia is not a solution. It is the same bow with a finer name. Mary is blessed among women. She is not a recipient of religious service. The honour due a fellow-servant is not a rung between latria and the rest of the church.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for hyperdulia. The term is medieval Catholic: a degree of religious honour above dulia and below latria, assigned to the Virgin. The Authorized Version does not know a third rank of worship.
webster_full: HYPERDULIA, n. [Gr. hyper, above, + douleia, service.]
A medieval Catholic rank of religious honour, above the dulia given to saints and below the latria given to God, assigned to Mary.
Not an 1828 English headword. The distinction is unknown to the second commandment and to the angel of Revelation 19:10.
The dictionary already has latria, dulia, and mariolatry. Hyperdulia is the middle name by which the bow is kept and the commandment is said to be kept also.
scriptures: Mat 4:10
Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.
Exo 20:3
Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
Isa 42:8
I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.

And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
But Peter took him up, saying, Stand up; I myself also am a man.
corruption_summary: A third rank of worship is invented so that the bow toward Mary can be called not-worship. Matthew 4:10 does not offer ranks. It offers only.
corruption_paragraphs: The catechetical move is always the same: we do not worship Mary, we give her hyperdulia. Latria is God's. Dulia is the saints'. She gets the extra. Matthew 4:10 does not read, “him only shalt thou serve, excepting a middle honour.” Him only. The angel of Revelation 19:10 will not take what a devout man thought was mere reverence. See thou do it not. Worship God. If the angel will not have it, the mother of the Lord will not have it either, and Luke never shows her receiving it.

Isaiah 42:8 is the end of the argument about images and about persons. My glory will I not give to another. A glory that looks like religious service — candles, invocations, titles of queen of heaven, prayers through her as mediatrix — is already another. Hyperdulia is the word that says it is not. The word is doing the work the commandment forbade.

Honour to Mary as the blessed among women, as the handmaid of the Lord, as a fellow-saint, is not the dispute. Peter said he was a man. So was she. The dictionary's mariolatry entry names the cult. Hyperdulia is the technical name the cult uses to say it is not a cult. Call the bow what the angel called it, and stop.
roots_summary: Greek hyper + douleia (G1397), service; proskyneō (G4352), to worship; latreuō (G3000), to serve; Hebrew abad / shachah.
roots_lines: Greek proskyneō (G4352) — to worship; Matthew 4:10, Revelation 19:10, the verb Rome splits into ranks.
Greek latreuō (G3000) — to serve; Matthew 4:10, him only.
Greek douleia (G1397) — bondage, service; the root of dulia and hyperdulia, which the New Testament never ranks as religious honours toward creatures.
usage: “Him only shalt thou serve” — not him, plus a middle rank.
“See thou do it not... worship God” — an angel refusing what Rome would call dulia.
“My glory will I not give to another” — a finer name does not make another less another.
